articles.title: City Council appoints Bonnie Tam as next Public Works Director
articles.author: Jake Lannon

blocks.text: The City Council voted unanimously on Monday, October 5 to appoint Bonnie Tam as Piedmont’s next Public Works Director. Tam brings nearly 20 years of local government experience in public works operations, capital improvement planning, and fiscal management. She most recently served as Public Works Director for the City of San Fernando and began her service with Piedmont on October 6.

“We are incredibly fortunate to have found someone with Bonnie’s depth and breadth of experience,” said Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen. “She’s led complex public works operations, managed major capital programs, and understands how to set priorities and make the most of limited resources. With so much important work underway throughout the city, Bonnie has the experience and the judgment to hit the ground running from day one.”

As Public Works Director in San Fernando, Tam led a full-service department and oversaw a $46 million Capital Improvement Program, including major infrastructure projects across water treatment, parks, and public facilities. Previously, at the City of Ontario, Tam oversaw a $690 million five-year Capital Improvement Program and led major initiatives including implementing an agency-wide asset management program.

Her municipal career also includes service with the cities of Monterey Park and Long Beach. Tam joins Piedmont at an important moment. The City has substantial needs across aging infrastructure and facilities. Meeting those needs will require careful prioritization, strategic use of local dollars, and maximizing opportunities to leverage outside resources.

Tam cites Piedmont’s engaged community as a major factor in her decision, saying “I was drawn to Piedmont because it is a close-knit community where people care deeply about their city and are involved in how it moves forward. My approach is centered on communication and collaboration – listening to residents, working across departments, and identifying and solving problems early.”

“I look forward to working with my colleagues and the community to preserve what makes Piedmont special while continuing to elevate the infrastructure and services residents rely on every day,” Tam said.

Tam holds a Master of Public Administration from the University of Southern California and a bachelor’s degree in Criminology, Law and Society from the University of California, Irvine. The City engaged Bob Murray & Associates to conduct the recruitment following the departure of former Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Rich Cunningham has served as Interim Public Works Director in Piedmont since former director Daniel Gonzales departed,

The salary for the Public Works Director is $237,029. This position includes reimbursement for professional development, a monthly auto allowance, and standard benefits associated with management team. These benefits include bereavement leave, personal leave, vacation leave, sick leave, and recognized holidays.

articles.title: Patch sales notch 1000 gourds for Wildwood
articles.author: Jay Russell

blocks.text: Pumpkin sales at the Wildwood Dads Club’s (WWDC) Pumpkin Patch are scorching hot this year, with more than 1,100 pumpkins, gourds and other items sold in the first 10 days. A big reinforcement, sure to tip the scales, is en route as well; Giant Jack will arrive this week.

When the giant pumpkin arrives patch visitors can pay $1 to guess Giant Jack’s weight. The closest guest will win possession and curbside delivery of the enormous gorgeous gourd for Halloween. Giant Jack will magically vanish from the winner’s home in November, courtesy of the Fuji Melons delivery team.

Patch Papa Matt Derrigo and his seventh-grade daughter, Sara Derrigo, both returned to the Patch this year as WWDC and Wildwood alums. The duo helped create a new fall photo spot for visiting families to create lasting memories. After years of visiting the Patch as an elementary school student, Sara is now helping shape the traditions and experiences for the next generation of Piedmont kids.
Opening weekend and the first full week of sales have substantially outpaced recent years, and this past Sunday brought in more than double the sales of the comparable Sunday last year.

“That growth is especially notable because Patch pricing has stayed largely the same for the past four years, so the increase is coming from more visitors rather than higher prices,” said Patch Papa Brian Fischer.
The high turnout is all the more impressive given this past weekend’s heat wave; temperatures in the 90s didn’t turn families away or smiles from patch visitors upside-down.

As of October 4, the Patch has sold 1,187 total items including 394 decorative pumpkins and gourds. Keeping the Patch open seven days a week, for five weeks requires 156 volunteer shifts and 90 Wildwood parents volunteers have already signed up to make the club’s biggest fundraiser of the year possible.

articles.title: Candidates’ Q & A – City Council Week 6
articles.author: Jake Lannon

blocks.text: Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions.

For this year’s race, the Post will send one question per week to the candidates running for City Council until Election Day. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on Tuesday, September 27, and were asked to reply in 200 words.
Week 6 question:

The police and fire departments are highly regarded amongst the public. According to the fire department’s union, they are asking for health benefits and retention pay to help recruitment and retention efforts. Would you, as a councilmember, support funding the union’s requests? If so, how would you fund these increased benefits?
Bill Reichle
(ReichleforPiedmont.com)

Piedmont residents I speak with consistently place a high value on public safety. Ensuring the police and fire departments have the personnel, training, and equipment they need — when they need them — will always be my top priority.

That is why I support local Measure GG on November’s ballot. Living in a high-cost metropolitan area with a competitive employment market creates inflationary pressure on the city budget, which limits management and personnel options. Measure GG is a well-thought-out solution to raise revenue that will stay here in Piedmont to fund essential services, including public safety.
Nancy Beninati
(NancyforPiedmont.com)

I support and appreciate the hard work of our police, fire, and city employees. I believe all Piedmont employees should be paid fairly and competitively, consistent with what the City can responsibly afford.

The City must carefully evaluate any proposals and the long-term fiscal impacts to make a decision that best serves our community as a whole. While Piedmont has some wealthy residents, the City’s revenue streams are limited and rely heavily on property taxes. Any significant increase in compensation or benefits must be considered in the context of the entire City budget, the needs of all City employees, and other important City priorities.

I support Measure GG because it would provide the City with additional ongoing revenue for parks, recreation, infrastructure, maintenance, and other City needs, including employee compensation. But additional revenue does not eliminate the need to make difficult budget choices.

As a councilmember, I would support fair compensation while also making sure that any agreement is financially sustainable and treats all of our employees fairly. Ultimately, the Council and City will have to balance competitive compensation with the City’s overall financial constraints and the priorities of the community.
Adam Hundt
(AdamHundt.com)

The City Council should present to the community a comprehensive plan for the police and fire departments. We need to maintain these services for the future in a way that is fair to the union members and ensures that the departments are adequately funded. Currently, overtime salaries are 136% of the amount approved for the budget year (a cost increase of $927,150). This is not sustainable for overtime firefighters or for the city.

Is the solution increasing the number of staff, changing the shift schedule, altering the duties (in addition to extinguishing fires, Piedmont firefighters are also trained as EMTs or paramedics), or something else? I believe everyone in the community deserves adequate health care. The plan the Council should produce must assure health benefits for the union and every other city employee.

Finally, we should explore ways to provide housing for Piedmont city employees. One way to do this is to work with developers to build below-market-rate units specifically for municipal employees such as firefighters, police, and teachers. I’m eager to work on this plan, and I promise to submit it to the whole community for comment.
Sunny Bostrom-Fleming

One of the main benefits of living in Piedmont is public safety. Protecting the lives of our families and our pets is our number one priority; our property can be replaced, but the lives we cherish cannot. While we are all very proud of both our police and fire departments, we must maintain a competitive workplace for these fine people.

Our current focus is the fire department. Where do we get the operator funds to make sure we are a very competitive community? Every day when they leave their homes they have no guarantee of returning alive or uninjured. Measure GG, which is vital to keeping our community financially sound, could go a long way toward funding the fire department. I want us to consider additional funding, such as the schools have with the Giving Campaign.

Seeing how we are surrounded by one of the most dangerous cities in America, Oakland reported 35,096 crimes in 2024: 6,000-plus auto burglaries, 1,100 residential burglaries, and 86 murders. Piedmont had 76 burglaries, one assault, and over 70 stolen cars. Our police and fire professionals are our first line of defense. The officers of Rome who led from the front lines earned their rank through merit and bravery.
Tom Ramsey
Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com)
Piedmont’s first responders are hometown heroes. While many families move here for the schools, we all value our top-quality police and firefighters who keep us safe every day.

As a small town, Piedmont is in a tough spot to match compensation packages offered by larger cities or towns that benefit from bigger budgets and commercial tax revenue. For decades, Piedmont navigated this position by determining salary levels through an independent third-party that conducts a salary survey comparing total compensation for each role against 13 Bay Area cities identified as comparable to Piedmont. Pay rates for each role are set based on the median compensation.

Recruitment challenges are regional, and responsible budgeting requires balancing new requests such as increased healthcare benefits with existing city obligations, where retiree and current employee medical premiums already cost the city $4 million annually.

I acknowledge this process is taking too long, and it weighs heavily on all involved. I am committed to continuing transparent, good-faith dialogue through our established bargaining representatives to reach a sustainable agreement that is both fair to all employees and fiscally responsible to the community.

articles.title: League of Women Voters hosts forum for City Council candidates
articles.author: Jake Lannon

blocks.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters hosted a Candidates Forum on Tuesday, September 29. The hour-long forum asked candidates running for City Council to respond to many of the community’s pressing questions. The five candidates running for three positions are Nancy Beninati, Adam Hundt, Tom Ramsey, Bill Reichle and Sunny Bostrom-Fleming.

For the first time in over six years, the LWVP hosted the forum in person for the community to attend. The forum was held in the City Council chambers of City Hall and was broadcast live through the league’s YouTube channel and KCOM.

LWVP volunteers Jennifer Giessler and Kathleen Quenneville served as moderator and timekeeper. The forum allowed each candidate to provide a two-minute opening statement introducing themselves, their credentials, and why they’re running for City Council.
After the opening statements, candidates were numbered 1 through 5, and the moderator called on them at random to answer each question. The candidates had a minute and a half to answer each question.

The questions were chosen from a public submission form and reviewed to ensure a wide range of topics. The forum asked candidates questions about Piedmont’s community, the budget, capital projects, infrastructure, disaster preparedness, and Automated Licence Plate Reader (ALPR) camera privacy.

At the end of the questioning period, each candidates presented a one-minute closing statement describing why Piedmont citizens should vote for them and directed the audience to resources that would inform them of their positions.
To watch the full forum and hear the candidates’ responses, readers can go to the LWVP’s YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/@lwvpiedmont/featured.

Visit the Election Resources page (https://bit.ly/4ymy5xS) to learn about what’s on the ballot and how, when, and where to vote. Ballots started going out to every registered voter on October 5. Ballot drop-off locations will open October 6. If you have moved or changed your party or your name, you can update your registration online. The last day to register to vote is October 19.

articles.title: City needs to fix hiring procedure at Fire Dept.
articles.author: Susan Goldsmith and Joseph Waxman

blocks.text: Editor:

We seek your assistance in making sure that Piedmont Firefighters are accorded salaries and health benefits in keeping with the fact that they are our Piedmont citizens’ extended family in terms of their dedication to our health and safety.

We moved to Piedmont in 1993 and raised our two children here. We have experienced the intelligence, caring and decision-making of our Piedmont Firefighters. Had we not personally benefited from the firefighters’ kindness and skill, we would still feel tremendous gratitude to them for being here just in case.

We were very distressed to read the article in the September 23 Piedmont Post indicating that negotiations between the firefighters and the city are at a standstill. We carefully read the firefighters’ concerns about the necessity of 1) having pay increases to encourage longevity, and 2) having retirement benefits to cover firefighters’ medical care for the period between retirement and Social Security eligibility. We share the firefighters’ underlying concern about inadequate staffing which requires excessive overtime to keep us safe.

As residents and taxpayers, we support the firefighters’ demands. Piedmont prides itself on being a city that is at the forefront of good decision-making. Piedmont needs to step up to support the firefighters and to inform its citizens what efforts and finances are required to do so. We rely on Piedmont Firefighters for our lives and the lives of our children. Is there anything more important? The firefighters’ knowledge, skills, courage and work ethic should be celebrated and honored by accepting their demands.

We are both retired attorneys; Joe represented injured workers and clients denied social security disability; I practiced civil rights law. As residents of Piedmont, we find the city’s response puzzling and extraordinarily short-sighted (using overtime instead of properly hiring, making the very hiring process discouraging by not providing the enticement of raises after certain years of service are reached, by not meeting the basic human need of health insurance until Social Security eligibility is reached).
We look forward to hearing from you.
–Susan Goldsmith and Joseph Waxman

articles.title: Yes on Measure GG
articles.author: Fran Bishopric Wolfe and Cameron Wolfe, Jr.

blocks.text: Editor,

We are writing to Piedmont voters to urge a YES vote on Measure GG. Our families planted roots in Piedmont more than 100 years ago. We have made our home here because Piedmont offers a unique combination of small-town ambiance with strong public safety, outstanding public schools and excellent quality of life amenities such as beautiful parks, strong recreation programs and lovely public spaces.

We believe the financial experts who are telling us we soon will have a shortfall in revenues to pay for existing city services, facilities and infrastructure. The cuts that will come if that happens, most likely starting with “quality of life” expenses, threaten the things we hold most dear about Piedmont.

We believe the small increase in the real estate transfer tax proposed by Measure GG is the most painless method of dealing with the threat. It is only imposed at a time when property is being sold—a time when funds are most likely to be available to make a payment. Your YES vote on Measure GG will help preserve the Piedmont that has kept our families here for so long.
–Fran Bishopric Wolfe and Cameron Wolfe, Jr.

articles.title: Support Measure GG: Support our community
articles.author: Kim Hunter

blocks.text: Editor,

My family moved to Piedmont for the schools AND for the public safety. Having a local police and fire department won’t protect everyone from all crimes and accidents, but knowing that our professional first responders have the ability to respond in 5 minutes or less is very reassuring.

These services are paid for by tax dollars which are allocated annually by our elected leaders, supported by volunteer financial experts, and professional city staff. The entire process is public and the proposed and approved budgets are posted on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. The budget reflects our community’s priorities of fiscal responsibility and public safety. This is reflected in the fact that the vast majority of operating expenditures go to the police, fire, and public works departments.

When people ask me what Measure GG will support, I tell them it will support what our community values. It will support all the things that make Piedmont a safe place to live and raise our families. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure GG.
–Kim Hunter Retired Alameda County Senior Deputy District Attorney

articles.title: Keep Piedmont moving forward with Measure GG
articles.author: Sara Lillevand

blocks.text: Dear Editor,

When I was young, Piedmont Recreation Department programs were instrumental in my development and helped form the person I am today. When I was fortunate enough to serve as Piedmont’s Recreation Director and later as City Administrator, I gained insight into the ongoing cost of the many services provided by the City of Piedmont to the community. From streets to parks, sidewalks to police cars, fire apparatus to building maintenance, the costs to provide essential services to Piedmont have continued to rise.

Piedmont is one of a small number of California cities whose revenues are primarily property based. This funding structure severely limits options for increased revenues needed to keep Piedmont from falling further behind. Measure GG is a reasonable way to provide additional and ongoing funds to support city services, while not placing an ongoing burden on property owners. If approved, Measure GG will bring Piedmont’s transfer tax more in line with our surrounding communities and provide approximately $1.5 million in additional revenue to support essential services and city infrastructure.
Piedmonters understand the value of ongoing investment, especially in community services and assets. Supporting Measure GG is a way to keep up and keep Piedmont moving forward for years to come.
Sincerely, Sara Lillevand Retired City Administrator

articles.title: Join us in supporting Adam Hundt

His platform strikes the right balance for our city’s future, placing emphasis on energy-efficient home upgrades, improved sustainability, and mitigating community risks from wildfires and other natural threats.

Adam will bring a fresh perspective, analytical approach, and creative problem-solving to Piedmont’s city governance. We’re excited to support his candidacy and encourage you to join us in voting for Adam Hundt for City Council.
Sincerely, Erin and Andrew Schultz

articles.title: Reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta Community College District Trustee, Area 5
articles.author: Teddy Gray King

blocks.text: Editor,

Having served eight years on the Piedmont City Council, including two years as mayor, I understand deeply that the true measure of public service is not the popularity of every individual decision; it is whether the institution is stronger, more accountable, and better prepared for the future when one’s service concludes. That is why I am again supporting Dr. Cindi Reiss for the Peralta Community College District Board.

When I endorsed Cindi in 2022, I noted her educational and accreditation experience, devotion to the common good, attention to detail, intellect and vision. I also recognized her willingness to challenge entrenched interests in pursuit of sound fiscal management. When she ran for the Board in 2018, Peralta faced serious financial instability, accreditation concerns, leadership turnover, board conflict, board micromanagement of chancellors and possible state-takeover of the district. Cindi Reiss has fulfilled those promises.

Today, Peralta is financially and institutionally stronger. Its four colleges are fully accredited. Stable executive leadership, stronger financial practices, greater transparency, and more disciplined long-range planning have replaced years of instability. Recent credit ratings reflect increased confidence in the District’s governance and financial direction, while a 2025 bond-refunding transaction saved taxpayers $13.7 million.

These gains did not happen by accident. Cindi helped foster a Board culture focused on its proper responsibilities: setting policy, safeguarding public resources, requiring accountability, and supporting strong professional leadership without micromanaging it. She has also demonstrated the courage to make difficult decisions when the district’s long-term interests required them.

But recovery is not completion. Peralta must now carry its Transformation Plan from vision into implementation. That means reducing fragmentation, coordinating programs and services, strengthening pathways for students, and building a fiscal structure capable of sustaining the colleges well beyond the tenure of any trustee or administrator.

As Piedmont residents, we have a direct stake in Peralta’s future, in its strength and success. Whether it’s through our many Piedmont high school students that have participated in dual enrollment with Peralta by taking Calculus III: Partial Differentiation, Discrete Mathematics, Linear Algebra or business management classes; adults that have taken art and language classes, or through the thousands of students that Peralta’s colleges serve in Alameda County, Piedmont benefits from a strong Peralta Community College system. When Peralta helps students earn degrees, certificates or transfer to universities, and build economically secure lives, the benefits extend well beyond its campuses.

A strong Peralta means a stronger regional workforce, greater economic mobility, responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars, and a healthier and more stable East Bay. Our support of Peralta’s colleges
is an investment in the regional institutions and quality of life on which Piedmont itself depends.
I urge my fellow Piedmonters to reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta Community College District Trustee, Area 5, on November 3.
Best, Teddy Gray King

articles.title: Voting information for the November 3 Election

blocks.text: On November 3, Piedmont voters will elect representatives to fill three seats on the Piedmont City Council and to federal, state, county, and special district offices. The ballot also includes a proposed increase to the City’s Real Estate Transfer Tax and 14 statewide ballot measures.

All registered Alameda County voters will receive a vote-by-mail ballot. The Registrar of Voters began mailing voter information guides on September 24 and will begin mailing ballots starting Monday, October 5. Sign up for the Registrar of Voters’ Track My Ballot tool to get notified when your ballot is mailed, received, and counted.

The last day to register to vote for the November 3 election is Monday, October 19. If you’re already registered, check your registration status before October 19 to confirm that your information is correct. You’ll need to re-register if you have moved, changed your name, or wish to change your political party preference. Voter registration forms are available at the City Clerk’s Office and from the Registrar of Voters. You can also register to vote online at registertovote. ca.gov.

In Piedmont, ballot drop boxes are near the mailboxes at Highland Way and Mountain Avenue and are available 24 hours a day. The Alameda County Sheriff’s Office picks up ballots from the drop boxes and returns them to the Registrar of Voters daily. The last pickup will be at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3.

If you mail your ballot through the post office, it must be postmarked by November 3 and received by November 10. Whether submitting your ballot by mail or a secure drop box, remember to sign the back of your return envelope – otherwise your vote will not be counted!

Alameda County voters can vote in person at any of 100 Vote Centers across the county. In Piedmont, the Veterans Memorial Building at 401 Highland Avenue will serve as a Vote Center. All vote centers will be open:

items: Saturday, October 31 – Monday, November 2: 9 a.m. - 5 p.m.

articles.title: Fire Dept. seeks community input on disaster preparedness

blocks.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is asking community members to complete a brief disaster preparedness survey by October 30. The survey will measure changes since 2024 and help guide future preparedness efforts.

Preparedness knowledge and actions have changed since the city’s first community survey in 2024. This survey will help the city understand how prepared the community is for earthquakes, wildfires, and other disasters.

The survey should take about 5-7 minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. The city’s 2024 survey showed that many respondents recognized disaster risk but had not taken some basic preparedness steps.
Among respondents:

items: 22% had a current household emergency communication plan
34% had a current two-week emergency water supply
27% felt confident or very confident in their knowledge of how to prepare for disasters

blocks.text: This year’s survey revisits many of these measures and includes new questions about how the city’s preparedness efforts have developed. This includes earthquake safety and steps that residents can take to minimize wildfire risks at home.
The survey will ask where people turn for information during an emergency, what gets in the way of becoming better prepared, and what kinds of resources would be most useful.
Since the 2024 survey, Piedmont Fire has expanded preparedness outreach and community engagement, including:

items: Updating Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan with extensive community participation
Increasing education about wildfire home hardening and defensible space, including a series of presentations to community groups
Conducting a practical wildfire evacuation exercise in the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood and creating an at-home evacuation exercise available to all households
Continuing year-round outreach on emergency alerts, evacuation readiness, and household preparedness

blocks.text: The survey data will help the city evaluate where the work is having an impact and what gaps remain. It will also establish a stronger baseline for earthquake preparedness as Piedmont Fire looks to expand outreach in this area.

Results will help guide future communications, educational resources, exercises, and community programs. Complete the survey by October 30 at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. For resources and information about preparing for disasters, visit piedmont.ca.gov/Disaster.

articles.title: City Council awards $785,000 contract for Moraga Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project
articles.author: Jake Lannon

blocks.text: At the September 22 City Council meeting, the Council voted to award the Moraga Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project contract to Terocons Inc. for $785,533. The project will install safety improvements as recommended in the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan. Construction is expected to begin in early October along Moraga Avenue between Ramona Avenue and Red Rock Avenue.

The project will install bulbouts and high-visibility crosswalk striping at the intersection of Ramona and Moraga. The intersection of Monticello & Moraga will receive a landscaped pedestrian refuge island and high-visibility crosswalk striping. The last intersection, Mesa & Moraga, will receive a bulb-out, flashing beacons, and a repositioned crosswalk for improved visibility.
Interim Public Works Director Rich Cunningham presented the project to the City Council, detailing some of the changes the project will make.

“The intersection between Moraga and Monticello, which you have to walk 120 feet across that intersection to cross it, was not safe, and so we’ve put a traffic island there. Part of that traffic island is set aside for landscape, and we’re bringing water across the street from the cemetery planted area via a pipe that will be installed before paving the Moraga Avenue section. The design also includes preservation of the bike lane,” said Cunningham.

The city will fund the project through an Alameda County Transportation Commission (ACTC) grant, which awarded the city $748,000 for design and construction. The ACTC funds transportation improvements throughout Alameda County that facilitate safe, efficient, and accessible travel for all types of transportation.

The City’s 2021 Safer Streets Plan identified the Mesa/Moraga intersection as the highest-priority location for citywide pedestrian safety enhancements, prioritizing intersections based on proximity to a school, location on an arterial street, and inclusion on a bike/bus route. Moraga Avenue is one of the few arterial roadways within the City of Piedmont eligible for regional transportation funding.
“There’s been almost uniform support across the community. We got a lot of nice emails, proactive people up and down Moraga who are all for it,” said Cunningham.
The contract agreement with Terocons Inc. is for 16 weeks to complete the work.

articles.title: Barbara Lee announces $5,000,000 in state funding for Fairyland
articles.author: Jay Russell

blocks.text: On Monday, October 5, Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee announced that Children’s Fairyland has secured a $5,000,000 allocation from the state of California to close out phase one of its capital investment in the park. The funds are designed to facilitate the initial stages of restoration and revitalization.
“It’s really a storybook that comes to life. Regardless of how old you are or young you are, my family can attest to the fact, this is a dream come true,” said Lee.

Children’s Fairyland CEO Kymberly Miller elucidated the details of the funding, $3,000,000 will be designated to the park’s capital investment to make “sure we are taking care of this physical space for 76 more years.”

The remaining two million will go to the park’s general operations. The funds come from the state’s budget which has allocated $14 million for Oakland community organizations, small businesses, public safety, and transitional housing.

Other Oakland institutions receiving state funding include: Juntos Fruitvale Cultural Arts Center, Samuel Merritt University’s human trafficking prevention initiative, commercial corridors across Oakland, the city’s Department of Violence Prevention and The Holland transitional housing facility.

“For 76 years, Fairyland has given Oakland’s children a place to imagine what’s possible. I still remember bringing my sons here, and today we’re making sure the next generation gets that same magic. This $5 million is a proud victory for Oakland because every dollar we put into community spaces comes back to us in the children they raise,” said Lee.

Children’s Fairyland has been a vital part of Oakland’s culture since opening in 1950. As the park that pioneered children’s entertainment in this country, Fairyland forever changed the landscape of “family fun” as it is known today. Children’s Fairyland is ten acres of green space on the shores of Lake Merritt, designed for outdoor play and low-tech, high-touch hands-on learning. It is a rare and increasingly precious resource for children.
The $5 million allocation will fund numerous initiatives within Fairyland’s strategic capital
investment plan, including essential infrastructure and facility upgrades. Miller describes the funding as foundational, rather than final.

“This funding is a launchpad, not a landing place. We have much more work to do to create the Fairyland of tomorrow. We’re deeply grateful to Governor Newsom, Mayor Lee, and our State of California partners for recognizing what Fairyland means to this community, to Oakland, and to the entire Bay Area. We are laying the groundwork for Fairyland’s financial sustainability so we can continue to be a safe and inclusive environment for playing and learning, where children build critical literacy skills and grow both socially and emotionally,” said Miller.

The state funding is a commitment to ensure the 76-year-old iconic and beloved Oakland destination remains a safe, vibrant, and accessible oasis for generations to come. It also signals a broader shift underway at Fairyland. As an organization upheld and supported by its community, admissions, memberships, and the generosity of donors of all kinds, Children’s Fairyland is now adding the kind of institutional support it needs to fuel the next phase of its modernization.
Learn more at Fairyland.org.

articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

blocks.text: Mocha is a 6-year-old Siamese mix who knows how to make herself at home. Although she’s guarded in new situations, when she’s relaxed, you might find her snoozing in a lap or accepting belly rubs. When she wants to play, you’ll love watching her pounce after her favorite wand toys, zoom through her tunnel, and tackle her tiny toy caterpillar.

That playful streak can occasionally get ahead of her manners: Mocha can switch quickly from cuddling to play mode, and may grab or swat at nearby hands. So she’ll do well with an adopter who has enough experience with cats to notice when to preemptively redirect her energy. She prefers to be the only cat in her kingdom, and takes daily anxiety medication to help her feel her best.

Give her the boundaries she craves, and the playtime she adores, and you’ll have a clever, affectionate companion who greets you at the door with little meows, rubs against your legs, and sleeps on your chest. Her foster sums her up simply: “She’s such a beautiful, sweet girl.”

articles.title: PHS holds annual Consent Assembly
articles.author: Julia Stokes

blocks.text: On Wednesday, September 30, Piedmont High School held its annual Consent Assembly for seniors and freshmen. The assembly, organized by acting teacher Kim Taylor, junior Stella Joseph, and senior Ben Ramakrishnan, involved current PHS students reading real stories from anonymous PHS graduates about their experiences involving sexual assault and consent.
“The purpose of the Consent Assembly is to bring awareness and educate people about how to stay safe and how to prevent these stories from happening again,” junior Ida Marshall said.

Marshall was one of 16 students who read stories. Although Marshall is enrolled in acting, students do not need to take acting to present in the assembly. A goal of the assembly is for people from across the school to be involved.
“I think it went well. All of the other story readers were really talented and I thought we made the stories sound really real. I heard stories about people being affected by it,” Marshall said.

PHS also has a lunch club, Piedmont for Consent (P4C), that focuses on spreading awareness about consent. According to P4C co-president junior Sophia Puckett, the club’s goal is to make sure everyone feels comfortable about consent and their personal boundaries.
Puckett said that club events this year include giving presentations about what consent is at elementary schools in Piedmont, along with partnering with an elective class at Piedmont Middle School.

“The middle school has a new class that’s going to help us lead presentations for the elementary school. It’s called LEAD,” Puckett said. “It’s an elective class, and it focuses on consent next semester.”
P4C co-president junior Lucy Shoop said that they are working on a middle school assembly as well.
“We’re working on a script that the middle schoolers are going to use in the new elective. Basically, we’re going to help them teach,” Shoop said.

The Consent Assembly happened to coincide with the reopening of a 2024 sexual assault case at Cornell University, which sparked conversations across the PHS campus. Puckett said that Piedmont for Consent held an open conversation at lunch for students to share their thoughts about the case.

“I think with the Cornell case, a lot of the stories and conversations can be triggering for a lot of people, and we want to make sure people have a place they can come if they need something,” Puckett said.
Although Piedmont for Consent is not directly affiliated with the Consent Assembly, Puckett said that their goals very much align.
“The assembly is a great way that we are getting the message of consent culture out to Piedmont and other Bay Area schools,” said Puckett.
The Consent Assembly takes place once a year, and Marshall said she hopes to continue her involvement.

“I really enjoyed doing it. I thought it was a really meaningful and valuable experience, and I hope I’m able to do it next year,” Marshall said. “I think bringing awareness to this stuff is not talked about enough and that’s why it’s really important.”
Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post.

articles.title: The season of the spider
articles.author: Dr. Megan Taylor

blocks.text: There are lots of signs that fall is arriving in the Bay Area. The days are getting shorter. Leaves are beginning to change. And in my family, we start looking for spiders.

Every year around this time, my kids and I search Golden Gate Park for shamrock orbweavers. They’re hard to miss once you know what you’re looking for: often in wait for prey at the center of giant, wheel-shaped webs— where their family name “orbweaver” comes from—these spiders’ large abdomens range in color from pale cream to bright orange, and their long legs are striped with light and dark colors. It’s no wonder local birds often notice them before we do!
I know for some of you, I’ve already lost you.

Spiders make plenty of people uncomfortable. But I’ve always loved them, and over the years my kids and I have made a tradition of getting closer rather than backing away. We find a few orbweavers each fall in the park and think of them as our “pets” for the season, returning regularly to watch them spin webs, grow, and change.

By the time we encounter these adult orbweavers at their biggest and most spectacular, they’re nearing the end of their lives. They’ve reproduced and left behind egg sacs containing the beginnings of another generation. And eventually, the spiders we’ve been watching disappear.
There is something both beautiful and sad about witnessing the cycle.

The natural world gives us countless opportunities to notice cycles of change. Flowers bloom and die. Leaves fall and return. Insects emerge and disappear. A spider reaches the end of its life, but leaves behind hundreds of eggs that will begin the cycle again.

This fall, I encourage you to look for opportunities to notice life changing around you, including the parts that may feel strange, uncomfortable, or even a little scary. Ask questions. Look closer. Come back tomorrow.
You might be surprised by what captures your curiosity.

If spiders still feel like too much of a stretch, perhaps monarch butterflies are more your speed. On October 24, join us for We All Journey (https://www.exploratorium.edu/visit/calendar/we-all-journey), a special day-time event at the Exploratorium exploring another remarkable cycle of life: the monarch’s transformation from caterpillar to butterfly and its annual migration to Mexico, where its arrival often coincides with Día de Muertos. Through art and hands-on activities, families can explore how cultures find meaning in the natural cycles of life, change, and renewal.
Whether it’s a spider or a butterfly, there’s a lot to learn when we take the time to look closely.

Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life.

articles.title: To take or not to take: that is the PSAT and preACT question
articles.author: Ayla Blanford

blocks.text: After years of colleges moving away from requiring standardized testing, the admissions process is shifting once again. As more universities reinstate SAT or ACT requirements, high school students are reconsidering the role tests, like the PSAT, play in their college preparation.

During COVID-19, many universities stopped requiring test scores as part of their application process, shifting to test-optional or test-blind. As testing gains popularity, many students view the PSAT as their first step of the college application process.
“I took the PSAT to get a baseline of what my score was without studying, so that I could compare it to my preACT score to see which one I was better at,” junior Chiara Silvio said.
Students often take these exams in their sophomore year of high school, so they can know which test they want to take and are most confident in junior year.
“I wanted to see which one I was better at so junior year I can really focus on studying,” sophomore Naomi Jerez said.
Although the PSAT has become increasingly popular, some students are choosing to use other resources to determine which direction they want to go in.

“I did not take the PSAT; I didn’t sign up for it because I plan to take the online ones at home,” junior Kyla Williams said. “I was also going to take the SAT in December, January, and another one in March.”
As top schools switch to being test-required, it affects students differently depending on their educational experiences and future goals.
“A lot of people study for it, and it’s not actually accurate, it’s more about the tools you have available to you than how well you’d naturally do,” Silvio said.

While preparation plays a large role in a student’s success when taking a standardized test, each student nationwide is taking the same test. This uniformity provides colleges with a baseline to help determine a student’s admission.
“Giving your grades or just your transcript only shows in comparison to your school,” Williams said. “For the SAT, it’s an overall evaluation that doesn’t solely compare to your surroundings.”
With the increase in resources available to students, standardized tests help colleges determine how a student truly performs.

“Nowadays you can get good grades by taking online classes, and get into a good school,” Jerez said. “With a standardized test, everyone’s taking the same thing, so it’s easier to compare scores objectively.”

Taking the PSAT and preACT is not a required step for the real SAT or ACT, and can take multiple hours depending on testing location. PreACT exams were conducted in the PHS STEAM building on Saturday, October 3, starting at 8:45 a.m. and lasting for two hours and 45 minutes.
“The test was really draining, and it was a lot harder than I thought it was going to be,” Silvio said.
However, many students say the benefits outweigh the effort required.
“I’ll be able to know which format I like better and I’ll also get an idea of the test taking environment,” Jerez said.
Along with prepping students for the SAT, taking the PSAT offers students a series of other benefits to support their college applications.
“You can sign up for National Merit, because it helps you qualify if you take the PSAT,” Williams said.

For the class of 2026, many universities have announced their switch from test optional to test required. Cornell University, Yale University, Columbia University and Princeton University are some of many that have announced their change. Many schools have also announced changes to their requirements that won’t take effect for a few more years. The University of California schools (UC Berkeley, UCSB, UCLA, etc.) are still test-free for the fall 2027 admission, and are reviewing whether or not to bring back testing for future applicants, according to the University of California.
Ayla Blanford is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern with the Piedmont Post.

articles.title: Bringing Harvest Festival scarecrows to life
articles.author: Jay Russell

blocks.text: Every year, Harvest Festival scarecrows are constructed by Piedmont students to be auctioned off in Piedmont Park during the event to fund the schools. The Havens TK pumpkin and 3rd-grade turkey scarecrows both started as giant balloons coated with several layers of Piedmont Post paper strips and wood glue before coming to life at the festival.

Normally, each grade at the three elementary school makes its own scarecrow, but this year some grades combined forces and others did not participate. Those that were on display were fantastic. The Havens creators of two of the seven scarecrows shared their process with the Post.

“Due to drying time, we could only apply a couple of layers per day, working over several weekends alongside some late-night prep work. My kids, Simone and Sloane, did a lot of the initial papier-mâché work before our scheduled class work parties,” said parent Holen Brady.

Brady shared that the main challenge was applying enough coats to dry thoroughly before the balloon lost air. One scarecrow had to be scrapped when a balloon deflated and distorted the shape. These two Havens scarecrows required three separate work parties, with 20 families in total participating.
“The kids really enjoyed the papier-mâché and painting, but the highlight for them is seeing their final product displayed at the Harvest Festival and knowing they helped create it,” added Brady.

These scarecrows are not heavy, but their size makes transporting them tricky. The Fedor and Moravy Havens families put on their trucker hats and transported the giant turkey and pumpkin scarecrows to the park and then to the auction winners’ homes.
This labor of love supports the schools while championing the arts, and the efforts of all scarecrow makers kept a beautiful Piedmont tradition alive.

blocks.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules:

articles.title: PHS volleyball team beats Castro Valley – first time since 2018
articles.author: Jonathan Comeaux

blocks.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team claimed a big 3-0 sweep of Castro Valley on Thursday, October 1 at Binks Rawlings Gym, improving their record to 14-8 with five matches left in the regular season. The victory marked the school’s first win over the Trojans since 2018, a testament to the program’s progress over the last two years.

“Castro Valley may have been undermanned, but we didn’t blink or let off. We had strong play in all three sets, and that’s what we want. The girls stayed really focused,” co-head coach Mike Glass said.

This year’s volleyball team is already among the school’s best in the last decade based its record. Their 14 wins is the most since 2017 when the team went 16-8. Other top teams in school history include 2013 when they went 19-11, the 2012 team (18-15), 2009 (22-9), and 2008’s all-time best team that went 24-6 and reached the D4 North Coast Section Championship.
Piedmont hasn’t won an NCS game since 2015, making that the goal of this year’s team.

“We’re making steady progress. There’s a lot we still want to work on, so we just want to keep doing our best to improve. I think we’re playing our best right now. We have moments where we lock in against our top competition, so we want to see that all the time,” Glass said.

“Year after year, the Piedmont program is strengthening more and more. In this game, we came out with a bunch of energy every single set. We just played our own game,” junior middle hitter Lucia Dorsey mentioned.

Against Castro Valley, PHS was without starting outside hitters Fiona Olsen and Sofia Meyer. It led to big games by Dorsey with 10 kills, Nora Trombi with seven kills, and Olivia Stevens with five. Glass called Dorsey’s performance her best of the season.
“Where a lot of the power came from was from Corina [Vora’s] sets. She encouraged some of our plays between me and Maika [Ting]. My chemistry with the setters is becoming super strong,” Dorsey said.
Match Recap
Piedmont won by scores of 25-21, 25-17, 25-17 over the visiting Trojans.

In the first set, Piedmont trailed 4-2 before scoring four straight points to take a 6-4 advantage and never relinquished the lead. Both teams traded points with PHS holding an 18-14 lead, then scored on three straight kills by Izara Dando, and two by Trombi. Castro Valley closed the gap to 23-20, but Piedmont scored two of the final three points with kills by Trombi and Dorsey.

PHS opened to a 5-1 lead in the second set, but CV battled back to take a 6-5 lead. The Highlanders regained the lead at 7-6 and maintained their advantage from then on. After that, Piedmont scored seven of nine points to take a commanding 14-9 lead and extended to 21-13. They finished with four of the closing eight points to win 25-17.

Castro Valley started with a 4-2 lead in the third set, but Piedmont took control with a run nine straight points with two kills by Maika Ting. CV inched closer to 12-7 but PHS scored three straight with kills by Ting and a block by Dorsey

Final stats: Ting had 13 kills and 11 digs. Charlotte Bailey had three kills, two blocks and one dig. Dando had three kills and seven digs. Trombi had seven kills and two digs. Stevens had five kills, two aces, and 14 digs. Dorsey had 10 kills, one ace, and one block.. Allyson Huynh had 16 digs and four assists. Corina Vora had two aces, nine digs and 25 assists. Hazel Schaeffer had 11 digs. Mia Bechtel had one ace, four digs and seven assists.

NEXT UP
Piedmont (14-8 overall, 3-2 league) hosts league rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 8 at 6:30 p.m.

articles.title: Athletes of the Month: Maika Ting & Henry Stein
articles.author: Jonathan Comeaux

blocks.text: We have now rolled through the first month of school. With our first Athlete of the Month of the new school year, we’re awarding Maika Ting of girls’ volleyball and Henry Stein of boys’ water polo our two Athletes of the Month for September. Honorable mentions go to Maddy Huynh of girls’ tennis and Dylan Jerez of boys’ water polo.
MAIKA TING

Maika Ting earns Athlete of the Month for September after leading the girls’ volleyball team in kills in every match this season. Some of her best performances include 24 kills and six aces in a 3-2 loss to Salesian on September 3, 13 kills and three aces in a 3-1 win over San Leandro on September 8, 17 kills in a 3-0 win over Encinal on September 22, and 16 kills in a 3-1 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on September 23.
HENRY STEIN

Henry Stein earns Athlete of the Month for September for filling the stat sheet in multiple categories for the boys’ water polo team. Some of his best games include nine goals, one assist, and two steals in a 12-11 loss to San Marin on September 19, five goals and three assists in a 9-8 loss to Clayton Valley on September 18, five goals and two assists in an 11-8 victory over Marin Catholic on September 18, and four goals, an assist, and three steals in a 14-6 win over Encinal on September 24.
Honorable Mentions

Maddy Huynh earns an honorable mention for making a huge impact on the girls’ tennis varsity roster as a freshman, typically appearing at No. 3 singles, which a few appearances in the No. 2 spot. In September, the freshman won eight matches and lost just twice – both of which went to an extra third set.

Dylan Jerez earns an honorable mention for his instant impact on the boys’ water polo team as their starting goalie as a sophomore. He had 12 saves, a steal, and assist in Piedmont’s 14-6 win over Encinal, 10 saves and five assists in a 15-11 win over Bishop O’Dowd on September 4, and nine saves in their 8-7 double overtime loss to James Logan on September 3.

articles.title: Girls tennis team tops College Prep, Castro Valley
articles.author: Jonathan Comeaux

blocks.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team won two of its last three matches last week. They beat North Coast Section foe College Prep 6-1 on Tuesday, September 29 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, but lost 4-3 to NCS rivals Head-Royce at home the following day. They wrapped up the week with a 6-1 Western Alameda County Conference win on the road over Castro Valley on Thursday, October 1.
The win over CV maintains Piedmont’s undefeated 3-0 league record. Head-Royce, was notably last year’s No. 9 seed in the D1 NCS Team Tournament, while PHS was No. 12.
“We’re still in the hunt for another league title, Alameda will be the competition. This was a good result against Head-Royce, they are a good team,” coach Jim Landes said.
Piedmont won last year’s WACC title with a 7-1 record. At 3-0, it sets up a critical October 14 match against the Hornets.

“We all really want it and have been playing really well as a team. We lost a lot of seniors from last year’s team, but I think we’re playing better than expected – at least for me, personally. But I think the team and myself is getting into a rhythm, so hopefully we can challenge for that title,” junior Leela Sivakumar said.
6-1 over College Prep
The Highlanders won all four singles matches and two of three at doubles.
At singles, Ella Ruthven won 6-0, 6-2 at No. 1. Faith Chin won 6-0, 6-3 at No. 2, while Maddy Huynh had a 6-0, 6-0 sweep at No. 3. Sivakumar won 6-2, 7-6 (7-5) at No. 4.

Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 1 doubles, while Layla Reed-Miguel and Mai Pham also had a double-bagel 6-0, 6-0 sweep at No. 3. Ella Thomasson and Paige Chin lost in three sets at No. 2, 4-6, 6-0, 10-3.

Piedmont won the three of the first four matches of the day, but lost the final three.

Amalia Angulo and Reed-Miguel fell 6-3, 6-1 at No. 3 doubles to start, but Piedmont ran off three straight wins after that. Sivakumar won 6-4, 6-2 at No. 2 singles, Huynh won 7-5, 6-1 at No. 3 singles, and Thomasson and Pham won 7-6 (7-3, 6-3) at No. 3.
Chan and Silvio lost 6-3, 7-6 (8-6) at No. 1 doubles, and Faith Chin fell 6-4, 6-2 at No. 2 singles.
It all came down to Ruthven at No. 1 singles, but she fell in a close three-set match, 6-2, 4-6, 10-7.

Piedmont won three of four singles matches. Ruthven won 6-1, 6-2 at the No. 1 spot, while Faith Chin won by the same score, 6-1, 6-2 at No. 2. Huynh won in a 6-0, 6-0 sweep at No. 3, but Sharafi lost 6-2, 6-1 at No. 4.

The Highlanders won all three doubles matches. Chan and Silvio won in three sets at the No. 1 spot, 6-4, 6-7 (7-5), 10-6. Reed-Miguel and Pham won 6-1, 6-1 at No. 2, and Welch and Oldrin won 6-3, 6-0 at No. 3.

articles.title: Water polo team suffers two losses
articles.author: Jonathan Comeaux

blocks.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team suffered two losses on the road over the past week, bringing their overall record to 6-8 overall and 1-2 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. articles.title: Piedmont competes in first league meet of season
articles.author: Jonathan Comeaux

blocks.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Point Pinole Regional Park in Richmond for their first Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season on Wednesday, September 30. The boys’ team finished fifth of nine schools, while the girls were fifth of eight.

“There were a lot of things to be encouraged about in these results. We had strong performances at the front of both teams, some very impressive performances from our younger runners, and, most importantly, quite a few runners making significant improvements. We still have plenty of work ahead of us, but it is great to see the training beginning to show up in the race results as we head into October,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said.

Senior running Alex Schleuning led things for the boys’ team, finishing seventh of 88 runners with a time of 16:26.1 on the three-mile course. It was the first time for the team to be led by a runner other than junior Dresden Schulte-Sasse in four events this season. Schulte-Sasse, meanwhile, was close behind Schleuning in 10th, clocking a 16:32.2.

“Alex Schleuning led Piedmont with a great race. Dresden Schulte-Sasse was right behind him 10th overall. Dresden improved by an impressive 53 seconds from his previous 17:25 on the same course,” Zirkelbach said.

Next in for Piedmont was sophomore Dylan Wallway finishing 17th in 17:12.1, while rounding out their best-five was freshman Cormac Ross in 40th in 18:19.1 and sophomore Blake Riif behind him in 41st, 18:29.4.

“Freshman Cormac Ross continued his strong first season, running 18:19 as our fourth Varsity runner. Blake Riiff also continued his significant improvement this season, taking 37 seconds off his previous three-mile time,” Zirkelbach said.

As for the girls’ team, they continue to work without star runners like Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, and Kelsey Coleman. Junior Viviane Oesterer placed 14th of 68 runners, clocking a time of 20:19.1, and has now led the Highlanders in three of its four events this season.
“On the girls’ side, Viviane Oesterer led Piedmont with a strong run. She improved her previous time on this course by 13 seconds,” Zirkelbach said.

Behind Oesterer was senior Cora Brozowski Schrader finishing 18th in 20:45.1, junior Nikita Gorelik in 27th in 21:00, sophomore Camille Hauser in 34th in 21:19.8, while senior Annie Thornton rounded out their best five times in 46th, 22:56.5.

“Viviane was followed by Cora Brozowski Schrader, Nikita Gorelik, and Camille Hauser. Our first four girls were separated by exactly one minute, which is great to see as this group continues to develop. One of the biggest improvements of the meet came from Annie Thornton, who ran nearly two full minutes faster than her previous time on the course,” Zirkelbach said.
NEXT UP

Piedmont competes in the 47th annual Asics Clovis Invitational at Woodward Park on Friday and Saturday, October 9-10. The boys’ varsity team runs at 7:40 a.m. on Friday, while the girls compete at 10:00 a.m. the same day.

articles.title: Flag football team dominates American 53-6
articles.author: Jonathan Comeaux

blocks.text: It was a big night for the flag football team when hosting American on Thursday, October 1, The Highlanders beat the visiting Eagles by a one-sided 53-6 score. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 7-8 overall and 6-4 against Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division competition.
With four games left in the regular season, Piedmont needs one win to assure a .500 league record going into the WACC tournament on October 20.

“To be honest, I have not even spoke about NCS yet to the team. We’ve talked about our record in league and what we want to accomplish in the league, so our focus has been that. What I did talk to them about tonight is getting to the line, being intense, getting out quickly, and being prepared at the line. That intensity takes us into the rest of the season,” coach Beth Black said.
One player who has emerged as a defensive leader is Nea Mafi as the team’s new starting safety.

She’s filling big shoes left by Class of 2026 starter Dahlia Osman, who finished her high school career with 24 interceptions. Mafi is often acting as the defense’s signal caller, communicating with her other defensive teammates before the snap. She had an interception returned for a touchdown against American.
“She is a leader when she’s on the field and on the sideline. She’s constantly watching the game, and that’s helping her improve,” Black said of Mafi.

“I’m the safety and the last line of defense. It’s important to keep up communication because I see what the game from a different angle at safety. In the beginning of the season, I wasn’t as communicative. I didn’t know exactly how to get my voice out, but I’ve gotten more and more comfortable with the team, so I slowly started to learn it’s okay to be loud,” Mafi said.
Game Recap

After American punted on its opening possession, Piedmont scored on its very first offensive play on a short pass to Naiya Alexander that turned into a 50-yard catch and run. The receiver weaved her way around three defenders to doge tackles on the play, sprinting to the end zone. PHS converted a one-point try on a pass from Edie Elmquist to Sydney Latvala to give them a 7-0 lead with 4:52 left in the first quarter.

With American pushed back to their own five, Piedmont’s next score was an interception returned for a touchdown by Nea Mafi with 2:59 left. Elmquist completed a pass to Alexander for the one-point conversion, making it 14-0.

PHS scored again with 1:22 left in the first. This time, Elquist found Latvala on a 15-yard pass, making it 20-0 after a missed extra point. American answered with its only touchdown with 7:01 remaining in the second quarter.

The Highlanders scored on its ensuing possession on a 10-play, 66-yard drive. They converted a 4th-and-3 in the process at the Eagles’ 23 with an eight-yard run by Mafi and capped off with a nine-yard quarterback keeper by Elmquist. They converted another one-point try on a pass to Latvala, now 27-6 with 2:30 left.

They scored again with 8:36 left in the third quarter on a six-play, 66-yard series. This time, Skye Prata Baack made a nice catch on a near 10-yard pass by Elmquist for the score, making it 33-6 after a missed conversion.
Piedmont’s final three touchdowns were not recorded due to an overlap in sports schedules. Details were not provided, but two scores were logged by Zoya Shulze and one by Latvala.

articles.title: Jaunts for a haunted Halloween
articles.author: Jonathan Comeaux

blocks.text: Spooky season has arrived with Halloween right around the corner. What better time to awaken some spooky history of around the area, including your very own town?
Here’s a look into a batch of locations with rumors of a spooky past.
Tyson Lake, Piedmont

Tyson Lake is a small reservoir located between private residences between La Salle and Sotelo Avenues, tucked quietly behind the Hampton Field. The location is not public property, but is the only body of water in Piedmont a few locals are known to reel out some carp.

On July 20, 1951, the Oakland Tribune published that the Alameda County coroner’s jury today recommended that Tyson Lake, an unused reservoir here, be either drained or properly fenced to prevent further accidents following the drowning of 17-year old James Richards four days earlier.

But near a year to the day of the first accident, a second victim on July 10 drowned in Tyson; 19-year old Donald Stracner after swimming with two other companions. World War 2 Navy diver John Haubner, who was a former Piedmont Police Officer, was called on to retrieve Stacner’s body.

“As search for the body continued, Police Chief William Pflaum said he will “definitely recommend that some action be taken to alleviate this menace to life.” He said that in view of the fact there have been two drownings in the lake within a year, “something must be done’,” wrote the Oakland Tribune, via HistoryofPiedmont.com.

Later on August 8 of 1952, the City of Piedmont sought out to determine the owner of Tyson Lake following the drowning of Stracner. City Council urged the 20 home owners surrounding the lake to erect a fence
Tyson Lake now sits quant and quietly behind the lush homes of Sotelo and La Salle.
Hayward Plunge, Hayward

Allegedly, a swimming instructor back in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps pitter pattering, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in all-white garb from head-to-toe during the day as a teenager.

Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to continue the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in the process through the hills of Green Belt Park.
Black Diamond Mines, Antioch

The Black Diamond Mines is a location of the White Witch or Wailing Witch, per urban legend. The story goes that a nanny was expelled from town in the 1870s for practicing witchcraft, only to turn up dead in the mines under suspicious circumstances. Other legend says a nanny, named Mary, was executed after being accused of witchcraft when all of the children under her watch died of illnesses.
Niles Canyon, Fremont

The Niles Canyon ghost is an urban legend about young woman who died in a horse carriage accident over 100 years ago, said to have occurred specifically on February 28 when horses were spooked by two oncoming automobiles—throwing her from the carried. Legend has it a vanishing hitchhiker walks the road on that day every year, looking to hitch a ride to San Francisco
Moss Beach Distillery, Moss Beach

Grab a bite, a drink, a spectacular view, and a haunting story at the Moss Beach Distillery slightly past El Granada and Half Moon Bay. The “Blue Lady” is a story from over 70 years ago, where a young woman had an affair with a handsome piano player at the restaurant, falling in love with him. The lady in blue was said to have been murdered by her betrayed fiancé while walking on the beach below the restaurant.
Redwood Road Preschool, Oakland Hills

This one is very peculiar. Slightly past the intersection of Pinehurst and Redwood Road, there is a former preschool with a gruesome history. Legend has it, a knife wielding murder in the early 80s slayed an entire class of preschoolers on the grounds. Other reports from the Gasden Times indicated a man, Alan Robert Baer, was shot by police on the preschool property in 1981. All that is left of the school is the foundation and a lone swing set, while people have reported paranormal experiences of children’s laughter, voices, and swings in full-motion as if the school yard was bustling.

articles.title: Festival Opera presents Mad Scenes at PCA on Oct. 25
articles.author: Allyson Aleksey

blocks.text: Festival Opera’s Salon Series continues October 25 with Mad Scenes, a concert featuring sopranos Aura Veruni and Lila Khazoum and pianist Daniel Lockert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.
The 4 p.m. performance will feature scenes from operas including Mozart’s Idomeneo and The Magic Flute, Verdi’s Macbeth, Donizetti’s Anna Bolena and Lucia di Lammermoor, and Ambroise Thomas’ Hamlet.

The program will explore the darker and more theatrical side of opera, with costumes by designer Marina Polakoff and props incorporated into the performance to help tell the stories. The concert is scheduled just before Halloween and will highlight the macabre and unhinged elements of opera.
Audience members are invited to attend in costume.
Veruni and Khazoum are both acclaimed sopranos who will perform the featured scenes with Lockert accompanying on piano.

The concert is part of Festival Opera’s three-concert Salon Series, which is presented at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series concludes November 22 with baritone Efraín Solís, making his Festival Opera debut, accompanied by San Francisco Opera pianist Marika Yasuda.
The Piedmont Center for the Arts is at 801 Magnolia Ave. in Piedmont.
Tickets for the October 25 concert are $40. Visit festivalopera.org/salon-series to purchase tickets.

articles.title: Autumn Lights Festival returns to Lake Merritt Oct. 15
articles.author: Allyson Aleksey

blocks.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 15.
Now in its 15th year, the three-night festival brings illuminated art installations to the gardens surrounding Lake Merritt. The event has drawn more than 12,000 visitors since its launch in 2012.

This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays throughout the gardens, along with live entertainment, an art market, children’s activities and food and beverage vendors. Additional activities include a costume contest for children and adults, an artist awards program and a kids zone. The festival’s food court will feature local food trucks and vendors, along with beer and wine gardens.

Proceeds from ticket sales benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a nonprofit volunteer organization formed in 2004. The organization works with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization and programming of the gardens at Lakeside Park.
The seven-acre collection of themed gardens includes the Bonsai Garden, Sensory Garden, Toddler Garden and Urban Edible Garden, among others.
FGLM volunteers provide maintenance assistance as the city’s gardening staff has been reduced over time. The Autumn Lights Festival is the organization’s largest annual fundraiser.
Tickets and additional information are available through the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt at https://gardensatlake-merritt.org/about/.

articles.title: Filoli’s “Nightfall Halloween” event runs through Nov. 1
articles.author: Allyson Aleksey

blocks.text: Filoli’s “Nightfall Halloween” event is underway at the historic Woodside estate, with more than 53,000 tickets sold across its fall programs following a sold-out opening weekend.

“Nightfall” runs now through November 1 and is open from 5:30 to 10 p.m. The Halloween event features more than 1,000 illuminated jack-o’-lanterns, more than 200 scarecrows, character actors, food trucks and Halloween-themed attractions throughout Filoli’s historic house and gardens.
New this year is a Witches’ Village in the redwoods, featuring a 20-foot witches’ cauldron, woven wicker witches, live banjo music and haunted railway conductors.
The new Haunted Railway includes more than 1,000 feet of track through the redwoods, with miniature houses and other handcrafted elements along the route.
Nightfall is in its third year as a large-scale Halloween event at Filoli. The event had sold more than 32,000 tickets before the end of summer, according to Filoli.

A Nightfall Champagne Lounge is also offered at 5:30, 7 and 8:30 p.m. The 60-minute experience in Filoli’s Historic Ballroom includes three pours from a champagne flight and admission to Nightfall. Filoli said the Champagne Lounge also provides admission on some nights when general admission tickets have sold out.

During the day, Filoli is hosting Autumn Days through November 1 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The daytime program includes a pumpkin patch, fall decorations, harvest games, seasonal food and drinks, and photo opportunities.
Tickets and information are available at www.filoli.org.

articles.title: SF Playhouse presents Peter Pan Goes Wrong
articles.author: Allyson Aleksey

blocks.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Peter Pan Goes Wrong, a comedy about an amateur theater company attempting to stage Peter Pan while a series of mishaps threatens to derail the production.

Written by Henry Lewis, Henry Shields and Jonathan Sayer, the play follows the fictional Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society as its members take on J.M. Barrie’s classic story. The production features flying rigs, sword fights and a crocodile, along with forgotten lines, malfunctioning scenery and rivalries that spill onto the stage.

The play is by the creators of The Play That Goes Wrong, which similarly follows a fictional theater troupe whose production goes increasingly awry. Peter Pan Goes Wrong premiered in London in 2013 before later moving to the West End and Broadway.

Susi Damilano directs the San Francisco production. The cast includes Greg Ayers, Joe Ayers, Maggie Mason, Christian McCooey, Ezra Reaves, Renee Rogoff, Patrick Russell, Sophie Schulman, Terrance Austin Smith, Jomar Tagatac and Phaedra Tillery-Boughton, among others.

The production runs through November 28 at San Francisco Playhouse, 450 Post St. in San Francisco’s Union Square neighborhood. Performances are Tuesday through Sunday, with evening and matinee performances on select days. The show runs approximately two hours and five minutes, including a 15-minute intermission, and is recommended for ages 8 and older.
Tickets and information for Peter Pan Goes Wrong and additional shows and musicals are available at sfplayhouse.org/.

articles.title: Music at Kohl Mansion opens 44th season with Escher String Quartet
articles.author: Allyson Aleksey

blocks.text: Music at Kohl Mansion will open its 44th season on October 18, with a performance by the Escher String Quartet, an internationally recognized chamber ensemble based in New York City.

The Escher String Quartet features Adam Barnett-Hart and Bryan Lee on violin, Pierre Lapointe on viola and Brook Speltz on cello. Formed in 2005 and named for Dutch graphic artist M.C. Escher, the quartet is known for performances combining technical precision, interpretive depth and a distinctive ensemble sound.

The program will feature three works from the string quartet repertoire: Haydn’s Quartet in G major, Op. 76, No. 1; Shostakovich’s Quartet No. 3 in F major, Op. 73; and Brahms’ Quartet in A minor, Op. 51, No. 2.

The Escher String Quartet serves as Artists of the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center and has performed at venues and festivals including Wigmore Hall in London, the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., and the Auditorium du Louvre in Paris.

The ensemble has received several honors, including an Avery Fisher Career Grant and Lincoln Center’s Martin E. Segal Award. Its recording projects have included the complete string quartets of composers Alexander Zemlinsky and Felix Mendelssohn.

articles.title: PEBCC celebrates “The Sound of Home” at 2026 benefit concert & auction

blocks.text: What does it mean to find your voice—and a place to belong? The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) will explore that question at its 2026 Benefit Concert & Auction, “The Sound of Home,” at 6 p.m. on Saturday, October 10, at the DoubleTree by Hilton Berkeley Marina. The evening will celebrate extraordinary young singers and the community of families, educators, alumni, volunteers, accompanists, and supporters who make their musical journey possible.

Led by award-winning Artistic Director Eric Tuan, the evening will feature performances by PEBCC singers, including the Ensemble Choir, along with two special guest soloists: alumna Kate Offer, a classical singer and conductor, and PEBCC singer Naomi Walker, who recently received the 1st Prize Solo Competition award at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival. For Tuan, a world-class choral education is about far more than learning to sing.

“Choral music is one of the most powerful ways for young people to build connections with each other and the world around them,” says Tuan. “Our singers learn to listen to each other, to share their voices in a way that empowers the whole team, and to explore different cultures and perspectives through the universal language of music. As our alumni remind us, those experiences last for a lifetime.”

At the heart of PEBCC’s mission is the belief that every young person should have the opportunity to experience that journey, regardless of financial circumstances. Financial assistance is central to the organization’s commitment to building a community where every singer belongs.
The benefit concert supports that mission while celebrating the full circle of community surrounding the choir.

“Our singers are part of a community much bigger than themselves,” says Tuan. “The transformative experiences singers experience wouldn’t be possible without the alumni who come back to teach and volunteer, the families who support them through the program, and the supporters who give so generously of their time, talent, and treasure to ensure every singer finds a home at PEBCC.”
Tickets are available at piedmontchoirs.org. PEBCC’s Online Silent Auction opened Saturday, October 3, at 9:00 a.m. and closes Sunday, October 11, at 11:00 p.m.

The 2026 Benefit Concert & Auction is made possible through the generous support of Bell Investment Advisors, Commercial Bank of California, and Anonymous Foundation.
