articles.title: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra announces 90th anniversary

blocks.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest youth orchestra and the second-oldest in the United States, announces its landmark 90th Anniversary Season, celebrating nine decades of guiding young musicians toward excellence through orchestral music, education, and community. The 2026–27 anniversary season will feature four concerts spanning music from across centuries and cultures.

Founded in Berkeley in 1936 by conductor Jessica Marcelli, when women conductors were exceedingly rare, YPSO enters its 90th season following a successful concert tour of Finland and Sweden in June 2026. From its Berkeley roots, the orchestra has grown to bring together young musicians from across the San Francisco Bay Area. Today, under Music Director and Conductor David Ramadanoff, YPSO continues a tradition of challenging young musicians with great orchestral repertoire while fostering accomplishment, community, and a lifelong passion for music.

“I’m very proud to be part of an organization that has been providing young people the opportunity to play great music for 90 seasons,” Ramadanoff said. “During my 38 years as Music Director, it has been exciting and heartwarming to help this orchestra develop into an outstanding ensemble capable of playing the wonderful and challenging music we have programmed this season.”

The season starts with the fall concert on Saturday, November 7, 2026, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. YPSO will open its 90th season with Shostakovich’s Festival Overture, Debussy’s Nocturnes, and Brahms’ Symphony No. 1.

The winter concert will take place on Saturday, February 20, 2027, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. The winter concert features Tchaikovsky’s Romeo and Juliet Fantasy-Overture, Gabriela Lena Frank’s Three Latin American Dances, and other works, including music by Ralph Vaughan Williams. The spring concert is on Saturday, May 1, 2027, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. They’ll play Verdi’s Overture to La forza del destino, Dvořák’s Symphony No. 6, and additional repertoire.

The season culminates on Sunday, June 6, 2027, at 3 p.m. (venue TBA) with a special 90th Anniversary Pops Concert, bringing together current YPSO musicians with alumni from across generations of the orchestra’s history. Former YPSO musicians will be invited to return, reconnect, and play alongside the next generation, celebrating the lasting community YPSO has built over nine decades.

The program is expected to feature Arturo Márquez’s Danzón No. 2 and a festive selection of audience favorites from stage and screen, creating a joyful celebration of YPSO’s past, present, and future. The 2026–27 season honors YPSO’s 90-year legacy by bringing together generations of musicians through the music and community that continue to connect them.

Enjoy all four concerts of YPSO’s 90th Anniversary Season and save with a season package. Season packages are on sale now. The season package price for General is $70, and Premium is $100. articles.title: Wednesday Walkers discover that “Nace is Nice!”
articles.author: Ken Hubbert

blocks.text: Braving another warm day on Sept. 30, the last day of the month, 50 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group and five of their canine companions gathered at the Exedra excited to see if Nace Avenue really is nice.

Leading our walk and tour was Pat Keller, a long-time Piedmont resident and Wednesday walker. Having lived on Nace Avenue for years, Pat was well qualified to relate the history of the area and provide information about some of the homes.

We began the walk heading in the direction of Dracena Park. As we walked through the park on our way to Nace, Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup noted that there are now four great horned owls in residence.

Nace is a tiny street with 27 houses. One unusual feature of Nace is that it’s L-shaped, making a 90-degree turn toward the middle. The street was named after Frank C. Havens’ secretary, John Nace. At the time, it was common to name streets after the people who were involved in developing the city. Nace is now a popular street for young families, with approximately 28 kids on it.

The first house we visited was 22 Nace. It was built in 1906 for $2,820. We were fortunate enough to encounter one of the owners, KT, who graciously invited us to come into her magnificent backyard. It’s a breathtaking and fun little surprise when you enter the rear. The first thing you notice is the immensity of the outdoor living space with beautiful views of Piedmont. In addition there was a hot tub surrounded by redwood decking, a wooden, round-shaped sauna with a cold plunge adjacent, and an outdoor shower. To top things off, an inviting outdoor cabana with sofas tempted some of the walkers to sit and relax.

Leaving 22 Nace, we walked down the street to 42 Nace, which has an uncommon flat roof. Pat explained to the group that a fire in the 1950s destroyed the original pitched roof which was then replaced by the flat roof.

Continuing just next door, we visited 46 Nace, the present residence of Dave and Kathy Yam. Known as the “Gibson house,” it was built in 1910 by the Fenton family of ice cream fame. The original house had lath and plaster walls and the beams were first generation old-growth redwood.

The Smith family moved in around 1912 and the home remained in the family until 1991 (79 years!). It is reported that they planted the large Catalpa tree out front, which is now a Piedmont Heritage Tree. However, a neighbor, Mrs. Gibson, claimed to have grown up at 46 Nace and her father planted the tree. Winnifred inherited the house and married Orrin Smith sometime between 1940 and 1950. They had no children, but all of the family celebrations were held at the house. Orrin was a wood shop teacher at McClymonds High School in Oakland and had a great workshop in the basement. The shelves and drawers for storing hardware were built by his students as a shop project.

Orrin and Winnifred remodeled the house extensively both inside and outside, excavating a basement and using the surplus soil to level the backyard. Next, they dug out the front and built a garage. In 1976, Winnifred started the “Nace is Nice” block party to celebrate the Fourth of July. The current owner, Kathy, inherited the block party tradition and revived it in the 1990s.

When Winnifred passed away, her sister Barbara became the executor of the estate. Barbara was the mother of one of Kathy Yam’s best friends. At the time, Kathy and her husband Dave were looking for a home to buy since their daughter Amy was about to begin kindergarten. Fortunately for Dave and Kathy, Barbara agreed to sell the house in time for Amy’s schooling.

Since moving in, Dave and Kathy have extensively remodeled the house: adding a deck to the back, building a second story, re-shingling, constructing interior stairs to the basement, and assembling a new roof for the garage. In 2021, the house received the Design Award in the Excellence in Architecturally Consistent Design Category from the City. The added garage was the winner of the City’s Excellence in Integrated Garage Design in 2024. Dave provided the group with ink-on-linen drawings of the original house plans, as well as two photo albums of the 1950 remodel.

Crossing the street to our final stop, we ended our tour at 35 Nace, the home of Greg and Pat Keller. Walkers were directed into a lushly landscaped backyard. Beneath a slatted roof arbor, a table of ice cold water, chocolate chip cookies and chocolate cake were waiting. Enough sustenance to fuel the walkers on their uphill hike back to their Exedra start.
All the walkers agreed, Nace is really nice!!!
For further reading, “Queen of the Hills: The Story of Piedmont, A California City” by Evelyn Craig Pattiani mentions on page 92 a Mabel Nace.

Walking on Wednesday meets weekly at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra. The program is free and open to the public. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.title: Savoie: France’s Alpine wines
articles.author: Pierre DuMont

blocks.text: High in the French Alps, where vineyards cling to steep slopes beneath snow-capped peaks, the wines of Savoie are gaining attention for their distinctive character and sense of place.

For generations, Savoie’s vineyards have been closely tied to the region’s mountain communities. Today, a new generation of winemakers is bringing renewed energy to an area once known primarily to French locals and Alpine holidaymakers. The result is a collection of wines that can be remarkably fresh, mineral-driven and unlike those produced in France’s better-known regions.

White wines dominate Savoie’s production, with the Jacquère grape playing a central role. Light-bodied and crisp, Jacquère produces wines with lively acidity and subtle floral and citrus notes, making them natural companions to local mountain cuisine. Altesse, another important white grape, produces the more structured and aromatic wines known as Roussette de Savoie. My favorite wine is Chignin-Bergeron, which is made from the Rhone Valley’s Roussanne grape.

The region also has its own red specialties. Mondeuse, a traditional local grape, creates deeply colored wines with bright acidity, peppery spice and dark-fruit flavors. Gamay and Pinot Noir are also planted, adding further variety to the region’s offerings.

Savoie’s geography is central to its identity. Vineyards are scattered across valleys and foothills, often at considerable elevations. The cool Alpine climate allows grapes to ripen slowly while retaining the acidity that gives the wines their characteristic freshness.

That freshness is particularly well suited to Savoie’s traditional foods: fondue, raclette, tartiflette and other rich mountain dishes. The wines cut through the richness of the cheese and potatoes, creating a pairing that reflects the region itself.

As interest in distinctive, terroir-driven wines continues to grow, Savoie is increasingly finding a place on the international wine map. Its bottles offer something increasingly sought after by modern wine drinkers: wines with a strong sense of origin, tradition and landscape.
Philippe Viallet: a family name in Savoie wine

At the foot of Mont Granier in France’s Alpine Savoie region, the name Philippe Viallet has become closely associated with the area’s distinctive wines. The family wine story began in 1966, when Marcel and Yvonne Viallet acquired a small vineyard in Apremont. Their sons, Pierre and Philippe, later continued the family business, with Philippe helping to develop it into both a wine producer and wine merchant.

The Viallet range reflects the diversity of Savoie’s mountain vineyards. Among its bestknown wines is Apremont, made from the Jacquère grape. It is a light, crisp and refreshing white wine with bright acidity. Another important wine is Chignin-Bergeron, made from the Roussanne grape and generally fuller and more aromatic, with flavors of ripe fruit and flowers.

Roussette de Savoie, made from the Altesse grape, offers another distinctive style, while the winery’s red wines include Mondeuse, one of Savoie’s traditional varieties, as well as Pinot Noir and Gamay.
The winery also produces Crémant de Savoie, a sparkling wine, along with rosé wines.

Philippe Viallet’s wines offer a taste of the Alpine landscape. Fresh, lively and closely connected to local grape varieties, they demonstrate why Savoie is attracting growing interest from wine drinkers looking for wines with a strong sense of place and a character of their own.
NV Viallet Crémant de Savoie
A sparkling wine made in the style of Champagne, this is light and refreshing, dry and crisp with tiny bubbles. At $13 a bottle it is an incredible bargain.
2024 G.G. Bouvet Roussette de Savoie

This is another of the Viallet labels and Roussette is their name for the Altesse grape. It is a charming white wine, clean and crisp with floral notes of honeysuckle and orange blossoms. On the palate it shows peach and apricot flavors. Perfect aperitif.
2024 Vialet Chignin-Bergeron

Chignin-Bergeron is the name in Savoie for the Roussanne grape from the Rhone Valley. It is my favorite of the Savoie wines. Richer and fuller and round in the mouth with good weight and structure. Flavors of melons and pears and a long lingering finish. Excellent effort.
2023 Clos de la Galeze Mondeuse

Mondeuse is related to the Syrah grape and makes the best red wines in the Savoie. It is medium-bodied with flavors of cherries and currants and moderate tannins. It has ample acid and should drink well for five years.

articles.title: The price of the prize: Why AKC dog sports are slowly dying
articles.author: Sierra Berrick

blocks.text: The world of competitive dog sports can be one of the most exciting for canine enthusiasts. There is the opportunity to meet fellow dog lovers, win awards for your pup, and spend quality time with them. Unfortunately, fewer and fewer new people are joining. Let’s examine a couple of reasons that may explain this, and hopefully drive current professionals in the American Kennel Club (AKC) world to make some changes.

Not everything is the fault of individuals, but of our infrastructure. Simply put, money is an issue. With the costs of operating training clubs and events going up just like the cost of living, many people are being priced out of dog shows. To enter a dog in AKC conformation, the majority of shows cost around $37 a day. To compete in a four-day show, that’s well over $100, not counting the cost of travel and food. Even newer sports, such as Fast CAT, demonstrate significant costs on their entry forms. In California, pre-entry for Fast CAT, which allows two runs per dog per day, costs between $28 and $35 per run. Considering this sport is entirely based on participation, the unfortunate truth is that people are now paying for their titles rather than needing to demonstrate excellence with their dog. For young people who may have bachelor’s-degree-level jobs, these prohibitively high entry fees make it impossible for them to get their foot in the door.

Lack of new exhibitors is a big concern, not just because it means dog shows are slowly becoming an event only for the wealthy, but because fewer competitors means fewer championship points and majors. The AKC point system is based on winning against a certain number of dogs, and with more competitors aging out than entering the sport, it will become markedly harder for individuals to achieve championship titles with their dogs.

Now let’s talk about attitude. Many people coming from pet backgrounds assume that all dog people are enthusiastic and kind. Unfortunately, this is not always so within the dog show world. Many new participants at dog shows report feeling unwelcome and unsupported. Although there is no clear reason for this, the idea of people simply being competitive does not fully explain it.

The high costs of entry, plus feeling excluded by veterans in the sport, unfortunately lead many new exhibitors to quit before they’ve really started. This means that it is up to the old-timers in dog sports to open their hearts to new competitors, and for new competitors to set the tone in the sport as welcoming going forward. Perhaps the American Kennel Club should consider the long-term results of pricing out exhibitors with these high entry fees. Only time will tell if dog enthusiasts are able to commit to these necessary changes.

Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.title: J. Ronald Pengilly

blocks.text: J. Ronald (Ron) Pengilly passed peacefully on September 28, 2026. Ron was born on May 5, 1934 to Joseph and Lillian Pengilly in Montebello, CA where he was raised. He leaves behind his beloved wife of 67 years, Margaret Ann (Margy) Pengilly, his daughter, Kathryn Ann Pengilly, son James W. Pengilly and seven grandchildren.

Ron was a straight A student throughout high school and college. He attended UCLA where he was a member of the Phi Beta Kappa academic honorary society and the Phi Gamma Delta fraternity while participating in student government. Boalt Law School (now named UC Berkeley Law) came next. While at Boalt he won the state Moot Court championship. During his law school years, he worked as a “hasher” at the Kappa Alpha Theta sorority where he met his future wife, Margy.
They were married in 1959 after they both graduated. In 1961, they moved to Piedmont where they raised their children and have lived for over 60 years.

Ron joined a small law firm in San Francisco after passing the bar in 1959. He was only the 5th person to join. The firm grew rapidly and changed names several times and expanded nation and worldwide. Pettit and Martin became its permanent name.

Ron’s specialty was real estate law at which he excelled. Examples of his successes include the Transamerica Pyramid, Rossmoor, and the relocation of the San Francisco produce market. He loved his law practice.
In retirement he enjoyed having more time to be with his family, traveling, reading, and playing bridge and golf with friends.
Private services for the family will be held.
For those who have asked please make donations to the charity of your choice.

articles.title: Piedmont Springs Hotel, circa 1871
articles.author: Gail G. Lombardi

blocks.text: Part 2 in a series

It all started with the water. It smelled awful, but it made his old joints feel better. In the mid-1850s, old Isaac Holmes dragged a bathtub down the ravine to the mineral springs on the side of the hill. Soaking in the mineral water helped to ease his rheumatism. When he died, the mineral springs were forgotten.

In the 1860s, these mineral springs (said to contain sulphur, magnesia, iodine and iron) were re-discovered in the ravine behind today’s Exedra, the current location of Bushy Dell Creek. Drinking or soaking in mineral water was believed to have great curative powers. These mineral springs were similar to the popular mineral waters in Calistoga, and they were only three miles from downtown Oakland.

Investors quickly saw an opportunity to develop the springs and build a hotel to accommodate visitors who came to “take the waters.” They selected the name “Piedmont,” meaning “foot of the hills,” thus securing the name of Piedmont to our locale. The investors formed the Piedmont Land Company to buy 350 acres around the ravine, build the hotel and sell any adjoining land not needed for the hotel purposes as residential lots.

In 1871, the Piedmont Springs Hotel opened near today’s Exedra as a first-class resort. The photo of the hotel shows only the northern portion of the building, which had two wings and was twice the size of the building as shown.

The hotel had a wide veranda, 20 first-class bedrooms and two suites, five dining rooms, telegraph service, and a Grand Saloon (for men only) with an elegant mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove. The ladies’ entrance allowed women to enter the hotel, avoid the saloon and proceed directly to the main dining room with its crystal chandelier, linen tablecloths and fine china.

The hotel quickly became a popular destination and drew visitors who passed a pleasant Sunday at Piedmont Springs, strolling the meandering paths to the mineral springs and enjoying an excellent lunch or dinner. The dining rooms served fresh meat from nearby ranches, milk and butter from Blair’s Dairy, and fresh fruit and vegetables from its gardens. The hotel also offered fine wine and liquor for those who did not care for mineral water. Fashionable San Franciscans would come for a week to escape the summer fog. Many hotel guests enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to buy land and build their homes here.

The hotel thrived until 1892, when a spark from a faulty chimney started a fire on the roof. Hotel guests watched helplessly as the hotel burned to the ground before firefighters could arrive from downtown Oakland. The site would not be empty for long... but that’s another story.

The mineral springs are still in Piedmont Park, but they were capped in the 1950s because the sulphur fumes offended many residents. The historical marker at the Veterans’ Building gives the location of the springs.
To learn more about Piedmont’s history, see the Piedmont Historical Society website: Piedmonthistorical.org.
Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on March 28, 2018.

blocks.text: Editor,

We proudly support the candidacy of Bill Reichle for City Council. As Piedmont residents for nearly 50 years, we’ve always been grateful for the dedicated service of our elected public officials — the people who step up to run for challenging offices, and the people with the integrity and the competence so critically needed to get important community work done, and done right.

Bill Reichle has our enthusiastic support because he represents the finest example of one of those step-up people: Motivated by nothing more than a wish to give back to his community, he accepts no outside donations and is self-funding his campaign. Just as important, he brings to his candidacy a rare set of critical skills for the Council post — an even and generous personality, and an unequaled career background in administrative management. No surprise, then, that Reichle’s candidacy has been endorsed not only by Piedmont’s current mayor, but by eight former mayors, as well.

Beyond all that, Bill Reichle has developed a thoughtfully progressive program that emphasizes Public Safety, Fiscal Discipline, and Community Engagement. We urge you to check it out in detail at ReichleforPiedmont.com.
Tim and Marian Nelson 237 Scenic Avenue

articles.title: Endorsing Adam Hundt for City Council
articles.author: Pamela Strike Fullerton

blocks.text: Editor,

I am writing to endorse Adam Hundt for Piedmont City Council. I first met Adam while assisting him with his home search in Piedmont. During that process, I quickly came to appreciate his gentle, thoughtful manner and the respectful way he communicated his priorities, traits that I believe are essential for local leadership.

Adam is an exceptional candidate whose unique, highly relevant perspective makes him a strong asset for our city. His impressive academic background includes a bachelor’s degree from Brown, an MBA, a master’s in industrial engineering from the University of Michigan, and a master’s in public policy from Johns Hopkins with a focus on clean energy. This rigorous educational foundation underscores both his sharp intelligence and his drive.

Adam and his wife are raising their two young children here, and one of them attends Havens Elementary. His interest in local government grew from a desire to help Piedmont increase energy efficiency, an initiative that would lower our carbon footprint while boosting property values. Both are critical. While these issues inspired his run, his vision for our city is much broader.

While the Hundt family is relatively new to Piedmont, I deeply respect Adam’s commitment to getting involved and sharing his professional expertise. We need the fresh perspectives and energy that young families bring to navigate the complex issues ahead, and I believe Adam Hundt is exactly the kind of leader who will serve our community well.
–Pamela Strike Fullerton, Realtor Ramona Ave.

articles.title: Support Nancy Beninati for City Council
articles.author: Cory Smegal

blocks.text: To the Editor:

I am writing to support Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council. I have known Nancy for more than a decade, and over the years I have had many opportunities to see firsthand her commitment to our community.

I met Nancy through the Piedmont League of Women Voters where she served as President. Nancy put a tremendous amount of time and energy into leading the League. She worked hard to make sure the League provided our community with thoughtful, balanced opportunities to learn about important issues and participate in local government. She was organized, prepared, and consistently went above and beyond in serving our community.

Having served on the Piedmont Unified School Board for eight years, I understand the commitment that public service requires. I have seen that same commitment in Nancy. She brings decades of public and community service experience, a willingness to listen and learn, and a genuine commitment to Piedmont and its residents. I know she will bring those qualities to her work on the City Council.
I am proud to support Nancy and hope you will join me in voting for her for City Council.
Cory Smegal Former Piedmont Board of Education President
